cover.headline: Quantum computing needs qubits that last. The team lays out **what scalable means** for error-corrected logic.

slides.title: Building bigger quantum computers is mostly about adding more physical qubits to the system.
slides.body:
The intuition is straightforward: more qubits mean more computational power. Scale up the hardware, scale up what you can solve.

But physical qubits are fragile. They lose information quickly, and utility-scale algorithms require error rates far below what any physical qubit can deliver on its own. You need something more robust to run long computations.

slides.title: The paper defines scalable logical qubits as units preserved by repeated error correction across four dimensions.
slides.body:
The team reports that scalable logical qubits must meet four coupled criteria: reliability through repeated quantum error correction, scale to hundreds or thousands of units, capability for fault-tolerant universal operations, and performance with low-latency real-time decoding and feedback.

These dimensions trade off against each other. Improving one can constrain the others, and applications will require managing all four simultaneously to run long, complex algorithms end-to-end.

slides.title: Without a shared definition of scalable, progress on logical qubits is hard to measure or compare.
slides.body:
Different research groups optimize different things. One might maximize qubit lifetime, another might prioritize operation speed, a third might focus on replicability. Without common benchmarks, you cannot tell which approach is advancing toward utility-scale computation.

This framework gives the field a common language. It does not solve the engineering problems, but it makes the path to solving them measurable across labs and platforms.

caveats: This is a preprint that has not been peer reviewed, so no independent expert has verified the work yet.
The paper proposes a definition and characterization framework but does not report experimental results testing it.

caption: Scaling quantum computers is not just about packing in more physical qubits. The fragility of those qubits means utility-scale algorithms need error-corrected logical qubits that can survive long computations. In this early paper, a team introduces a definition of scalable logical qubits characterized along four dimensions: reliability, scale, capability, and performance. The framework is designed to make progress measurable and comparable across different quantum computing platforms. Published in arXiv as a preprint. The work proposes a definition without experimental validation. Full study: http://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20549v1 — Send this to the person in your life who keeps asking when quantum computers will actually be able to do something useful.

unsupported_claims.claim: The intuition is straightforward: more qubits mean more computational power. Scale up the hardware, scale up what you can solve.
